topic_title: Top 7 Best Low-Energy Dog Breeds for Calm and Peaceful Living
intro: Low energy means a dog that settles easily indoors, not one that needs no exercise. Every breed here still needs daily walks, usually 20 to 45 minutes, plus some play to stay healthy and avoid weight gain, which is a common problem in relaxed breeds. For a truly calm home, barking matters as much as energy: a quiet dog that naps all day can still disrupt the peace if it announces every delivery. Grooming is the other daily cost to weigh, since several of these breeds have long coats.

picks.description: The Japanese Chin is the best match for calm living because it is quiet in both senses: rated low for energy and low for barking. It weighs roughly 7 to 11 pounds, so it fits a studio as easily as a house, and short daily walks of 20 to 30 minutes plus a little indoor play cover its exercise. Chins are affectionate and gentle, get along with children, cats and other dogs, and tend to be reserved with strangers rather than noisy about them. They groom themselves in a cat-like way, and the silky coat needs only a weekly brushing, though it sheds moderately. Training is moderate; Chins respond to gentle repetition and dislike being forced. The flat face means they should not exercise hard in hot weather. The breed is uncommon, so expect a wait for a puppy.
picks.best_for: Quiet homes and apartments wanting a small, calm, rarely barking companion
picks.quirky_fact: Chins often wipe their faces with their front paws, a habit that gives them a cat-like reputation.
picks.skip_if: You want a walking partner for long hikes or a hardy dog for rough play

picks.description: The Sussex Spaniel is the slow, steady member of the spaniel family: rated low for energy and low for barking, with a gentle, calm temperament. It is a medium dog, long and low to the ground, and is content with around 30 to 45 minutes of unhurried walking a day, though it enjoys following a scent at its own pace. Sussex Spaniels are friendly with children, cats and other dogs and bond closely with their household. The long, wavy golden-liver coat sheds moderately and needs brushing a couple of times a week, with attention to the feathered ears and feet. Training is moderate; they learn well with patience and food rewards but are not quick to obey. This is one of the rarest breeds in the dataset, so finding a puppy can take a long time.
picks.best_for: Patient owners wanting a calm, medium spaniel for a quiet household
picks.quirky_fact: Unlike most spaniels, the Sussex was bred to work slowly and close to the hunter, which explains its unhurried pace today.
picks.skip_if: You need a dog quickly or want a fast learner for sports or tricks

picks.description: The Clumber Spaniel is the largest dog on this list and one of the most relaxed. It is rated low energy and low barking, with a gentle, loyal and calm nature, and it gets along with children, cats and other dogs. Daily needs are modest for its size: 30 to 45 minutes of steady walking, with no need for running. The trade-offs come from that size. A Clumber is heavy-boned and can weigh as much as a small adult can comfortably lift, so it needs room indoors and a car that fits it. The dense white coat sheds moderately and needs brushing a few times a week, and many Clumbers drool and snore. Weight control matters because extra pounds strain the hips. The breed is rare, and lifespan runs about 10 to 12 years.
picks.best_for: Houses with space wanting a large, mellow, quiet dog
picks.quirky_fact: Clumbers take their name from Clumber Park, an English estate where the breed was developed.
picks.skip_if: You live in a small apartment or mind drool, shedding and snoring

picks.description: The Shih Tzu is the easiest of the calm breeds to find and one of the lowest-energy dogs in the dataset. It needs only 20 to 30 minutes of gentle walking and indoor play a day and is happy to nap near you for much of the afternoon. It is affectionate and friendly with children, cats and other dogs. The trade-off is grooming: the long silky coat sheds little but mats quickly, so it needs daily brushing or a short clip every four to six weeks, plus regular eye cleaning. Barking is rated medium, usually at the door, and house-training can take longer because the breed is stubborn. The short muzzle makes it sensitive to heat. Lifespan is long, typically 10 to 16 years, which means a calm companion for many years.
picks.best_for: Apartment dwellers wanting a widely available, low-exercise lap dog
picks.quirky_fact: The breed's name is usually translated as lion dog, a nod to its long, mane-like coat.
picks.skip_if: You will not keep up with daily brushing or regular grooming appointments

picks.description: The Maltese is the smallest dog here, a toy breed usually under 7 pounds, and its exercise needs match its size: a couple of short walks and indoor games are enough. It is gentle, affectionate and playful in short bursts, gets along with children, cats and other dogs, and is rated easy to train, which helps with house rules and a quiet cue. Barking is rated medium, so it may announce footsteps in a hallway. The long white coat sheds very little because there is no undercoat, but it needs daily brushing or a short puppy clip with regular trims, plus cleaning around the eyes to limit tear staining. Its tiny size makes it fragile around rough play. Maltese prefer company and do not like long hours alone.
picks.best_for: Calm adults in small homes wanting a tiny, low-shedding companion
picks.quirky_fact: The Maltese is one of the oldest toy breeds, kept as a companion in the Mediterranean for over two thousand years.
picks.skip_if: You have toddlers who play roughly or are away from home all day

picks.description: The Basset Hound is famously relaxed indoors and rated low energy, with a gentle, friendly temperament that suits children, cats and other dogs. It is a medium-height but heavy dog, and around 30 to 45 minutes of slow walks a day keeps it fit; it would rather sniff than run. The short smooth coat needs only weekly brushing, though it sheds moderately, and the long ears need regular cleaning to prevent infections. Two trade-offs place it lower on this list. It is rated hard to train because its nose overrides instructions, so it must stay on a leash, and its bark is a deep, carrying bay that neighbors will notice. Bassets also gain weight easily, which strains their long backs, and they handle heat poorly.
picks.best_for: Easygoing households with a fenced yard wanting a mellow, friendly hound
picks.quirky_fact: A Basset's long ears help sweep scent up from the ground toward its nose as it walks.
picks.skip_if: You want an obedient off-leash dog or have close neighbors sensitive to noise

picks.description: The Tibetan Spaniel is small, low energy and calm, but it is more independent and watchful than the other breeds here. Short daily walks and some play are enough, and it often chooses a high perch such as a sofa back to watch the room. It is affectionate with its family and gets along with children, cats and other dogs, though it can be reserved with strangers. It ranks last because it is rated alert with medium barking, so it will announce people outside, which is less suited to a truly quiet home. Training is moderate; independence means it may ignore commands it finds pointless. The long coat sheds moderately and needs brushing once or twice a week. It handles cold well and lives about 12 to 15 years.
picks.best_for: Owners wanting a small, calm dog that is content with some alone time
picks.quirky_fact: Tibetan Spaniels were kept in monasteries, where they reportedly watched from walls and barked to alert the monks.
picks.skip_if: You need a dog that stays quiet when people pass the door

faqs.question: What is the calmest dog breed for a quiet home?
faqs.answer: On this list, the Japanese Chin is the best fit for a quiet home: it is rated low for both energy and barking, is small enough for any apartment, and gets along with children, cats and other dogs. The Sussex and Clumber Spaniels are equally calm and quiet, but they are larger, rarer and harder to find from breeders.

faqs.question: Do low-energy dogs still need daily exercise?
faqs.answer: Yes. Low energy describes how easily a dog settles, not how much activity it needs to stay healthy. Most breeds here need 20 to 45 minutes of walking a day plus some play. Relaxed breeds such as the Basset Hound and Clumber Spaniel gain weight easily, and extra weight puts strain on their joints and backs.

faqs.question: Which low-energy breeds are best for apartments?
faqs.answer: The small breeds suit apartments best: the Japanese Chin, Shih Tzu, Maltese and Tibetan Spaniel. The Chin is the quietest of them. The Shih Tzu, Maltese and Tibetan Spaniel are rated medium for barking, so early training on a quiet cue helps in buildings with shared walls. The Clumber Spaniel is calm but large for most apartments.

faqs.question: Are low-energy dogs good for older owners?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, because short walks and a calm temperament suit a slower pace. Weigh size and grooming too: a Maltese or Japanese Chin is easy to lift and handle, while a Clumber Spaniel can weigh as much as a person can comfortably manage. Long-coated breeds need regular brushing or professional grooming visits, which adds ongoing cost.

faqs.question: Can a low-energy dog be left alone during the day?
faqs.answer: Calm breeds tend to rest while you are out, but no dog should be alone for very long days without a break. The Tibetan Spaniel is the most independent breed here. Companion breeds such as the Maltese and Japanese Chin prefer company, so a midday visit or dog walker helps on long workdays.

seo_title: Low-Energy Dog Breeds for a Calm Home (2026)
answer: The Japanese Chin, Sussex Spaniel and Clumber Spaniel are the calmest picks here: all are rated low energy and low barking, and all get along with children, cats and other dogs. The deciding factor is size, since the Chin fits any apartment while the two spaniels need more room.
method: We filtered a 150-breed dataset for breeds rated low energy and good with children, cats and other dogs, then ordered them by barking level, size and trainability, putting the quietest, easiest breeds first.
